in_scope_clauses.summary:
8 risk management principles — integrated (part of all
activities), structured + comprehensive, customized (tailored
to org context), inclusive (stakeholder engagement), dynamic
(responsive to change), best available information, human +
cultural factors, continual improvement.

Risk management framework — leadership + commitment +
integration into governance + design + implementation +
evaluation + improvement of the framework itself. Distinct
from the risk management PROCESS (§6) which is the operational
execution.

Risk management process — communication + consultation; scope
+ context + criteria; risk assessment (identification +
analysis + evaluation); risk treatment; monitoring + review;
recording + reporting. Iterative across the lifecycle.

Integration — risk management is integrated into ALL
organizational activities + functions. Not a separate
function; embedded in strategy + governance + decision-
making + operations. ISO 31000 + ISO 31010 (risk assessment
techniques) together provide the meta-framework supporting
domain-specific risk standards (ICH Q9 / HARA / TARA /
HACCP / etc.).

Policies for information security — defined, approved by management,
published, communicated to and acknowledged by relevant personnel
and interested parties, and reviewed at planned intervals or when
significant changes occur.

Legal, statutory, regulatory, and contractual requirements relevant
to information security shall be identified, documented, and kept
up to date. The organization's approach to meeting each shall be
defined.

Separation of development, test, and production environments —
including separation of duties where appropriate — to reduce the
risk of unauthorized access or unauthorized changes to the
operational environment.

in_scope_clauses.section: Annex SL high-level structure (HLS) — common to all Annex SL standards
in_scope_clauses.summary:
Shared high-level structure — Annex SL HLS provides common
clause numbering across all ISO management-system standards:
§4 Context of organisation; §5 Leadership; §6 Planning;
§7 Support; §8 Operation; §9 Performance evaluation;
§10 Improvement. Common-clause identical text + discipline-
specific sub-clauses. IMS implementation leverages HLS for
single integrated documentation + single integrated
management review.

Shared policy + objectives — integrated quality + environment
+ OH&S + energy policy statement reflecting commitment to
all in-scope management systems. Per-MS objectives consolidated
into single objectives register; common cascade to operational
KPIs. Top management single signoff covering all included MSes.

Shared context + interested-party analysis — single context
analysis covering organisational external + internal issues
relevant to all included management systems; single
interested-parties register noting per-party expectations
across quality + environmental + OH&S + energy + IS scopes.

Integrated risk + opportunity register — single risk register
capturing quality risks (ISO 9001 §6.1) + environmental
aspects + impacts (ISO 14001 §6.1.2) + OH&S hazards + risks
(ISO 45001 §6.1.2) + IS risks (ISO 27001 §6.1.2) + energy
review-derived risks (ISO 50001 §6.3) + others. Common risk
assessment methodology (often ISO 31000-aligned). Composes
cleanly with iso-31000 meta-framework overlay.

Combined management review — single meeting + record covering
all in-scope MS-specific inputs per each standard's §9.3
(audit results, customer feedback, process performance,
nonconformities + corrective actions, monitoring + measurement
results, risk + opportunity status, supplier performance,
etc., plus MS-specific inputs like environmental performance,
OH&S performance, energy performance, IS performance). Outputs
consolidated into integrated improvement actions.

Combined audit programme — internal audits planned per ISO
19011:2018 covering multiple management systems in single
audit visits where practical. Auditor competency requirements
cover all in-scope MS standards. External certification body
may offer combined IMS certification audit (multi-MS audit
day-rate reduction; common observations resolution; single
integrated audit report).

Integrated documented-information control — single document-
control SOP covering all MS scopes; integrated document index
mapping documents to applicable MS clauses; common version
control + approval + distribution + retention rules. Single
records-retention SOP covering MS-specific retention
requirements (e.g., training records, calibration records,
incident records).

Annex SL HLS version tracking — ISO/IEC Directives Part 1
Annex SL revised periodically (Edition 2 in 2018; further
revisions ongoing); MS standards adopt revised HLS at next
standard revision. IMS implementation tracks per-MS standard
revision adoption + plans coordinated transitions
(e.g., ISO 9001 next revision; ISO 27001:2022 already
adopted Annex SL Edition 2 HLS).

Principles relating to processing — (1)(a) lawfulness fairness
transparency; (1)(b) purpose limitation (specified explicit
legitimate); (1)(c) data minimisation; (1)(d) accuracy; (1)(e)
storage limitation (no longer than necessary); (1)(f) integrity +
confidentiality (security); (2) ACCOUNTABILITY — controller
responsible for and able to demonstrate compliance with (1).
Accountability is the meta-principle behind ROPA (Article 30) +
DPIA (Article 35) + records discipline.

Lawful bases for processing — at least one of: (1)(a) consent;
(1)(b) contract performance; (1)(c) legal obligation; (1)(d)
vital interests; (1)(e) public interest; (1)(f) legitimate
interests (controller's or third party's, not overridden by
data subject's rights). Special-category data (Article 9) +
criminal-conviction data (Article 10) require additional
conditions. Lawful basis must be documented + communicated in
privacy notice (Articles 13-14).

Conditions for consent — freely given + specific + informed +
unambiguous indication by statement or clear affirmative action.
Demonstrable (controller must show consent obtained); withdrawable
as easily as given; written form requirements distinguishable
from other matters; bundled-consent prohibition; performance of
contract cannot be conditional on unnecessary consent (Article
7(4)).

Special categories of personal data — racial/ethnic origin,
political opinions, religious/philosophical beliefs, trade-union
membership, genetic, biometric (for identification), health,
sex life or sexual orientation. Processing prohibited unless
one of 10 derogations (9(2)(a) explicit consent through (j)
research/statistics with safeguards). Most adopter-relevant for
medical-devices (patient health) + pharma (clinical trial
participants) + HR (health/disability info).

Modalities for exercising data subject rights — controller
provides info in concise transparent intelligible easily-
accessible form, plain language. Response within 1 month
(extendable 2 months for complex requests with notification).
Free of charge unless manifestly unfounded or excessive (then
reasonable fee OR refusal with justification). Identity-
verification proportionate.

Information to data subjects — provided at collection (Article
13 when from subject; Article 14 when from third party). Required
content: identity of controller + DPO contact; purposes +
lawful basis (legitimate interests detail if used); recipients
+ transfers (international transfer safeguards); retention
period; existence of rights (access / rectification / erasure /
restriction / object / portability / consent withdrawal / DPA
complaint); automated-decision-making + profiling logic and
consequences.

Substantive rights — Article 15 access (copy + categories +
purposes + sources + automated-decision logic); Article 16
rectification; Article 17 erasure (right to be forgotten) with
6 grounds + 5 exceptions; Article 18 restriction (4 grounds);
Article 19 notification to recipients of rectification/erasure/
restriction; Article 20 portability (structured commonly-used
machine-readable format; direct controller-to-controller
transmission where technically feasible); Article 21 object
(legitimate-interests + direct-marketing absolute right);
Article 22 automated individual decision-making + profiling.

Data protection by design + by default — technical + organisational
measures implementing data-protection principles (e.g., data
minimisation) effectively + integrating necessary safeguards
into processing. By default only personal data necessary for
each specific purpose are processed. Amount + extent + storage
period + accessibility all subject to default-minimisation.

Records of Processing Activities (ROPA) — controller maintains:
(1)(a) controller + DPO + joint-controller + EU rep contacts;
(1)(b) purposes; (1)(c) categories of data subjects + personal
data; (1)(d) categories of recipients incl. international;
(1)(e) third-country transfers + safeguards; (1)(f) retention
schedule; (1)(g) Article 32 technical + organisational
security measures. Processor ROPA per Article 30(2). Exemption
under Article 30(5) for orgs <250 employees IS LIMITED (only
where processing is occasional AND not high-risk AND not special-
category) — most orgs in scope.

Security of processing — appropriate technical + organisational
measures considering state of the art + costs + nature/scope/
context/purposes of processing + risks to rights. Article 32(1)
illustrative measures: pseudonymisation + encryption; ensuring
confidentiality + integrity + availability + resilience of
processing systems; ability to restore + access after incident;
regular testing + evaluation of effectiveness. Maps cleanly to
ISO 27001 Annex A controls (compose with iso-27001 overlay).

Personal data breach notification — Article 33 controller
notifies supervisory authority within **72 hours** of becoming
aware unless unlikely to result in risk to rights + freedoms.
Notification content: nature of breach + categories + approximate
numbers of data subjects + records concerned + DPO contact +
likely consequences + measures taken. Article 34 notification
to data subjects WITHOUT UNDUE DELAY when HIGH RISK to rights
+ freedoms (unless one of 3 exceptions). Documented incident
record per Article 33(5) regardless of notification threshold.

Data Protection Impact Assessment — required when processing
LIKELY to result in HIGH RISK to rights + freedoms,
particularly: (3)(a) systematic + extensive evaluation by
automated means incl. profiling with legal/significant effect;
(3)(b) large-scale special-category or criminal-conviction
data; (3)(c) systematic monitoring of publicly accessible area
on large scale. Each supervisory authority publishes positive +
negative list of processing types. DPIA content: systematic
description of processing + purposes + legitimate interests;
necessity + proportionality assessment; risk assessment to
rights + freedoms; measures to address risks. DPO consulted
where designated.

Data Protection Officer — designation mandatory when (37)(1)(a)
public authority/body, (b) core activities require regular +
systematic monitoring of data subjects on large scale, or (c)
core activities consist of large-scale processing of special-
category or criminal-conviction data. Tasks per Article 39:
inform + advise; monitor compliance; advise on DPIA; cooperate
with + be contact point for supervisory authority. Article 38
position: involved in all DPP issues; provided with resources;
independent (no instructions on tasks; no dismissal for
performing tasks); reports to highest management.

Transfers to third countries / international organisations —
transfer permitted only if: (45) Commission adequacy decision
(currently incl. UK + Switzerland + Israel + Japan + Korea +
New Zealand + Andorra + Argentina + Canada commercial + Faroe
Islands + Guernsey + Isle of Man + Jersey + Uruguay + US under
EU-US Data Privacy Framework 2023); OR (46) appropriate
safeguards (Binding Corporate Rules, Standard Contractual Clauses
(2021/915), approved codes of conduct, certification mechanisms);
OR (49) specific derogations (consent, contract necessity,
important public interest, legal claims, vital interests, public
register). Post-Schrems II (C-311/18): transfer impact assessment
(TIA) required to evaluate destination country surveillance laws
vs. essential equivalence to EU rights.

Right to know — consumer may request disclosure of: categories
of personal information collected; categories of sources;
business or commercial purposes; categories of third parties
shared with; specific pieces of personal information collected.
Look-back period: prior 12 months (24 months effective
2025-2026 per CPRA regulations). Response within 45 days
(extendable +45 with notice). Two free reports per year.

Right to delete — consumer may request deletion of personal
information business has collected from them. Business must
delete + direct service providers + contractors + third parties
to delete. **9 exceptions** including: complete transaction;
detect security incidents; debug/repair errors; exercise free
speech; CalECPA compliance; public-interest research with
ethics review; internal uses reasonably aligned with consumer
expectations; compliance with legal obligation; internal
lawful uses compatible with collection context.

Right to opt-out of sale + sharing — consumer may at any time
direct business not to sell or share personal information.
Two-link or single combined-link notice methods per §1798.135;
"Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information" + "Limit the Use
of My Sensitive Personal Information" required where applicable.
Global Privacy Control (GPC) signal must be honored as opt-out
under §7025 of CPPA regs. 12-month opt-in waiting period before
requesting reconsent.

Right to limit use of sensitive personal information (SPI) —
consumer may direct business to limit use + disclosure of SPI
to that necessary to perform services or provide goods reasonably
expected. SPI categories: SSN, driver's license, financial
account + login credentials, precise geolocation, racial/
ethnic origin, religious/philosophical beliefs, union
membership, contents of mail/email/text not directed to
business, genetic data, biometric for identification, health,
sex life or sexual orientation.

Right to correct — consumer may request correction of inaccurate
personal information. Business must use commercially reasonable
efforts to correct. Effective from CPRA (2023-01-01).

Methods for submitting requests + response — two methods
(toll-free phone for offline + online form/email for online-
only businesses). Identity verification per §7060-7064 CPPA
regs (3-2-1 tier model — 3 data points for high-risk, 2 for
medium, 1 for low). 10-day acknowledgement + 45-day response
(extendable +45). Authorised agent provisions.

Notice at collection — provided at or before collection.
Required content: categories of personal information to be
collected; purposes for which used; whether sold or shared;
retention period per category; SPI categories collected +
whether used for purposes other than those allowed under
§1798.121; link to privacy policy. Just-in-time disclosure
for new categories.

Service provider + contractor + third party — contractual
restrictions distinguish service-provider relationship
(broader permitted uses for business purposes) vs. third-party
sale/share relationship (requires opt-out). Required contract
terms include: limit processing to business purposes specified
in contract; certification of compliance with CCPA; assistance
with consumer requests + cybersecurity audits + risk assessments;
flow-down to sub-processors; deletion-on-termination + audit-
rights. Maps closely to GDPR Article 28 DPA but distinct
categorization scheme.

Private right of action for data breach — consumer may bring
civil action for unauthorised access + exfiltration + theft +
disclosure of nonencrypted + nonredacted personal information
resulting from business's violation of duty to implement +
maintain reasonable security procedures + practices appropriate
to nature of information. Statutory damages: $100-$750 per
consumer per incident OR actual damages, whichever greater.
30-day cure notice required (does not apply when actual harm).
Class actions permitted.

CPPA regulatory regime additions — three regulatory packages
finalising 2025-2026: (1) **Automated Decision-Making
Technology (ADMT)** regulations — pre-use notice + opt-out +
right to know logic for "significant decisions"; (2) **Risk
Assessment** regulations — required when processing presents
significant risk to consumer privacy (analog to GDPR DPIA);
(3) **Cybersecurity Audit** regulations — annual audit by
independent auditor for businesses whose processing presents
significant risk to security. Applicability thresholds vary
by regulation.

Anti-bribery governing-body responsibility + senior-management
responsibility — the governing body (where one exists) shall
take overall responsibility for the ABMS, ensure its
establishment + maintenance, and approve the anti-bribery policy.
Senior management shall demonstrate leadership + commitment to
the ABMS.

Anti-bribery policy — top management establishes a documented
anti-bribery policy that prohibits bribery; complies with
applicable anti-bribery laws; is appropriate to the purpose +
context; includes commitments to satisfy ABMS requirements,
continual improvement, ability of personnel to raise concerns
in good faith without fear of reprisal; communicated to
personnel + business associates; available publicly where
appropriate.

Anti-bribery compliance function — top management designates an
anti-bribery compliance function with appropriate competence +
status + authority + independence + resources. Reports directly
to the governing body / senior management with appropriate
access.

Actions to address risks + opportunities — ABMS risks +
opportunities determined to give assurance that the ABMS can
achieve intended results + prevent / reduce undesired effects
+ achieve continual improvement.

Due diligence on personnel — for positions exposed to more than
a low bribery risk, due diligence shall be conducted on
candidates + on personnel transferring into such positions. Re-
conducted on a reasonable periodic basis or on suitable trigger.

Awareness + training — anti-bribery awareness + training
provided to all personnel appropriate to the bribery risk faced
in their roles. Specific training for higher-risk roles.
Records of training maintained.

Due diligence on transactions, projects, activities, business
associates + personnel — risk-proportionate due diligence
conducted before engagement (transactions, projects, activities,
business associates) and periodically thereafter. Higher-risk
engagements receive enhanced due diligence.

Financial controls — controls over financial transactions to
reduce bribery risk: segregation of duties, authorization
limits, two-signature requirements, controls over cash + cash
equivalents, expense + reimbursement controls, controls over
gifts + hospitality + donations.

Non-financial controls — procurement + commercial + operational
+ HR controls to reduce bribery risk: documented procurement
criteria, competitive bidding, conflict-of-interest disclosure,
controls over hiring + promotion + termination, controls over
contractor + agent appointments.

Implementation of anti-bribery controls by controlled
organizations and by business associates — risk-proportionate
requirement for business associates (Medium + High risk) to
either implement equivalent anti-bribery controls or commit
contractually to the organization's ABMS. Audit rights for
verification.

Gifts, hospitality, donations + similar benefits — controls
ensure such activities are not, and cannot reasonably be
perceived as, bribery. Pre-approval thresholds, documented
register, recipient + purpose disclosure, alignment with
organization's policy + applicable law.

Raising concerns — procedures encouraging + enabling personnel
+ business associates to raise concerns in good faith
(whistleblowing channel); anonymity + confidentiality
protection; non-retaliation; investigation; escalation to
compliance function.

Investigating + dealing with bribery — procedures for
investigation of suspected bribery + non-compliance with the
ABMS; authority + independence of investigators; preservation
of evidence; escalation to law enforcement where required;
disciplinary + corrective + preventive action.

Review by anti-bribery compliance function — periodic review
of the ABMS by the compliance function; reporting to top
management + governing body; consideration of changes to the
ABMS as a result of the review.

Business continuity policy — top management establishes a
documented policy that is appropriate to the purpose; provides
framework for setting BC objectives; includes commitment to
satisfy applicable requirements + continual improvement of the
BCMS; communicated within the organization + available to
interested parties.

Actions to address risks + opportunities — for the BCMS, to
give assurance that the BCMS can achieve its intended outcomes
+ prevent / reduce undesired effects + achieve continual
improvement.

Business continuity objectives + planning to achieve them —
consistent with policy + measurable where practicable +
monitored + communicated + updated. The BC objectives are
derived from the BIA.

Business Impact Analysis (BIA) — systematic process to identify
+ assess the impacts of disruption on prioritized activities;
determine prioritized activities + their resource requirements
+ identification of dependencies; determine prioritized
timeframes for resumption (RTO + MAO + MBCO + RPO).

Risk assessment — identify + analyze + evaluate risks of
disruption to prioritized activities. Outputs inform selection
of BC strategies + solutions (§8.4).

Business continuity strategies + solutions — selected to meet
RTO/RPO/MBCO targets per BIA; cover protection of prioritized
activities + their resources (people, information +
communication technology, infrastructure, supplies, partners
+ suppliers, financial resources). Stabilization, continuity,
recovery, return.

Business continuity plans + procedures — documented procedures
to ensure continuity of prioritized activities during disruption
+ respond to + manage the disruption; specific to types of
disruption per the risk assessment + BC strategies; reviewed +
tested + maintained.

Exercise programme — exercises (tabletop, communications
cascade, technical, full-scale) at planned intervals to
validate the BCMS; clearly defined aims, objectives, scope,
success criteria; post-exercise review with documented
improvements; varied scenarios over time.

Evaluation of business continuity documentation + capabilities
— periodic + post-disruption + post-exercise review of the
effectiveness of BC strategies, solutions, plans, procedures.

Internal audit — planned audits of the BCMS at planned
intervals; consideration of importance of processes + previous
audit results; auditor objectivity + impartiality; corrective
action.

Management review — top management reviews the BCMS at planned
intervals; inputs include audit results, BC exercise results,
changes in interested-party needs, risk + opportunity
identification, performance information, status of corrective
actions.

Nonconformity + corrective action — react to NC; evaluate
need for action; implement; review effectiveness; update BCMS
if necessary.

Understanding the organization and its context — internal +
external issues relevant to the QMS purpose + strategic
direction. Documented in a context-of-the-organization
analysis (often the opening section of the quality manual).

Quality management system + its processes — process approach,
including determining processes needed, their sequence +
interaction, criteria + methods for operation + control,
resources, responsibilities, risks + opportunities.

Leadership and commitment — top management demonstrates
leadership via accountability, customer focus, integration
of QMS into business processes, promoting process + risk-
based thinking, ensuring resources, communicating QMS
importance, engaging + supporting people, promoting
improvement.

Quality policy — established by top management, appropriate
to the organization's purpose + context, includes commitment
to satisfy applicable requirements + continual improvement,
provides a framework for setting quality objectives,
documented, communicated, applied, available.

Actions to address risks + opportunities — determined for the
QMS based on §4.1 context + §4.2 interested-party requirements.
Planned actions integrated into QMS processes. Effectiveness
evaluated. The "risk-based thinking" core of ISO 9001:2015.

Resources — people, infrastructure (buildings, equipment,
transport, ICT), environment for process operation
(physical, social, psychological), monitoring + measuring
resources (with traceability per §7.1.5.2 where applicable),
organizational knowledge.

Measurement traceability — when measurement traceability is a
requirement or considered essential, measuring equipment shall
be calibrated + verified against measurement standards
traceable to international or national measurement standards;
identified to determine status; safeguarded against
adjustments + damage + deterioration.

Communication — relevant internal + external communications
including on what, when, with whom, how, and who
communicates. Customer communication per §8.2.1.

Documented information — creation + updating + control of
documented information required by the QMS + by the standard.
Identification + description, format, review + approval,
distribution + access + retrieval + use, storage +
preservation, control of changes, retention + disposition.

Operational planning + control — plan + implement + control
processes needed to meet requirements for products + services,
including determining requirements, establishing criteria,
determining resources, implementing control of processes per
criteria, determining + keeping documented information
needed to confirm processes have been carried out as planned.

Control of externally-provided processes, products + services
— supplier controls. Type + extent of control determined by
potential impact on product conformity, effectiveness of
supplier's controls, ability to provide processes meeting
requirements. Supplier evaluation + selection + monitoring +
re-evaluation; flow-down of requirements; verification of
received product.

Production + service provision — implemented under controlled
conditions: documented information defining characteristics of
products + activities + results; suitable monitoring +
measuring resources; monitoring + measurement at appropriate
stages; suitable infrastructure + environment; competence +
qualification of persons; validation + periodic revalidation
of processes where resulting output cannot be verified by
subsequent monitoring + measurement; preventing human error;
release + delivery + post-delivery activities.

Post-delivery activities — determined by statutory + regulatory
requirements, potential undesired consequences of products,
nature + use + intended lifetime of products, customer
requirements, customer feedback. Includes warranty provisions,
contractual obligations such as maintenance services, final
disposal + recycling.

Control of nonconforming outputs — identified + controlled to
prevent unintended use + delivery. Actions: correction,
segregation, containment, return + suspension of provision,
informing customer, obtaining authorization for acceptance
under concession. Documented information retained on
nonconformity + actions taken + concessions + authorities
that decided actions.

Monitoring + measurement + analysis + evaluation — determine
what needs monitoring + measuring, methods, when, results-
analysis cadence. Evaluation of QMS performance + effectiveness.
Customer satisfaction (§9.1.2) monitored. Analysis +
evaluation results used as input to management review.

Internal audit — conducted at planned intervals to provide
information on QMS conformance + effective implementation +
maintenance. Audit program planned, established, implemented,
maintained, considering importance of processes, changes,
previous results. Auditors objective + impartial; corrective
actions taken without undue delay; documented information
retained.

Management review — top management reviews QMS at planned
intervals for continuing suitability, adequacy, effectiveness,
alignment with strategic direction. Inputs: status of actions
from prior reviews, changes in external + internal issues,
info on QMS performance + effectiveness (customer satisfaction,
objective achievement, process performance, conformity of
products, nonconformities + corrective actions, monitoring +
measurement results, audit results, supplier performance),
resource adequacy, effectiveness of actions on risks +
opportunities, opportunities for improvement.

Nonconformity + corrective action — when nonconformity occurs
(including from complaints): react, evaluate need for action
to eliminate causes, implement, review effectiveness, update
risks + opportunities, make changes to QMS if necessary.
Documented information retained on nature of NC + actions
taken + results.

Common Criteria — control environment + communication +
information + risk assessment + monitoring + control activities
+ logical + physical access controls + system operations +
change management + risk mitigation. Required for any SOC 2
examination regardless of category. Maps closely to ISO 27001
Annex A controls but with attestation-focused framing.

Security Trust Services Category — the foundational + mandatory
TSC for any SOC 2. Information + systems protected against
unauthorized access (logical + physical) + unauthorized
disclosure of information + damage to systems that could
compromise availability + integrity + confidentiality + privacy
of information.

Availability TSC (optional) — information + systems available
for operation + use as committed or agreed. Includes capacity
monitoring + disaster recovery + business continuity. Composes
with iso-22301 BCMS overlay.

Processing Integrity TSC (optional) — system processing is
complete + valid + accurate + timely + authorized to meet the
entity's objectives. Particularly relevant for financial
transaction processing + data-pipeline integrity.

Confidentiality TSC (optional) — information designated as
confidential is protected. Distinct from Privacy (which covers
personal information specifically). Composes with iso-27001.

Privacy TSC (optional) — personal information is collected +
used + retained + disclosed + disposed of to meet the entity's
objectives. Maps to GDPR + CCPA + sectoral privacy regs.

Type I vs. Type II — Type I is point-in-time control design
examination; Type II is operating-effectiveness examination
over a period (typically 6-12 months). Customers + adopters
expect Type II for ongoing service relationships.

Type II scope — attestation by independent CPA firm covering
BOTH (i) suitability of design of controls + (ii) operating
effectiveness of those controls OVER the specified observation
period. Auditor opinion covers both dimensions.

Observation period — minimum 3 months per AICPA guidance;
**6-month** for first Type II; **12-month** for subsequent
annual renewals. Continuous observation — gaps in observation
window weaken auditor opinion. Sample-based testing of
controls over the period — auditor selects samples per
population characteristics.

Renewal cadence — annual continuous attestation typical.
Common observation window: 11/1-10/31 (Q4-Q3) OR
10/1-9/30 (fiscal year). Auditor's report ready ~30-60
days after observation period end. "Gap letter" or bridge
letter optionally issued by auditor for the period between
observation-period-end + next-report-availability covering
no-material-change-occurred.

Enterprise customer default — Type II is the de-facto
enterprise-customer SOC 2 requirement. Procurement teams
typically reject Type I. Vendor management programs require
annual Type II refresh. SLAs sometimes specify a maximum-age-
of-current-Type-II-report (e.g., 12 months) as a contractual
requirement.

Control failures over the observation period — auditor
may issue modified opinion: (i) qualified — material control
failures isolated to specific area; (ii) adverse — pervasive
failures; (iii) disclaimer — unable to obtain sufficient
evidence. Most adopters target unqualified opinion;
management response section documents remediation of
identified failures + recurrence-prevention actions.

Shared responsibility model — both CSP and CSC roles + duties
explicitly identified + agreed in cloud service agreement.
Traditional ISO 27001 SoA + risk treatment plan extended to
cover responsibility-allocation per service model (IaaS / PaaS /
SaaS) + deployment model (public / private / community /
hybrid). Customer reviews CSP's SoA + responsibility-matrix at
onboarding + annually + on material service change.

Cloud-specific control — relationship between cloud service
customer + cloud service provider. CSP documents service-
specific responsibility allocation; CSC verifies + supplements
with customer-controllable security measures. Documentation
maintained for audit trail.

Virtual environment controls — segregation of virtual machines
/ containers / tenants per multi-tenant model (CLD.9.5.1) +
hardening of virtual-machine configuration (CLD.9.5.2). Network
micro-segmentation, hypervisor escape prevention, container
image scanning, host-OS hardening, secure-by-default templates.

Data removal at service termination + admin operations
monitoring — CSP-documented data-deletion process at service
termination (covers active + backup + replicated data); CSP
logs administrative operations performed on customer data +
makes logs available to customer. Critical for GDPR Article
28(3)(g) deletion/return obligations + GDPR Article 28(3)(h)
auditability.

Alignment of security management for virtual + physical
networks — when virtual + physical networks coexist, security
management is consistent + aligned. Virtual-network controls
not weaker than physical-network controls; visibility +
monitoring extends across both layers.

Customer-side supplementary controls — even where CSP
operates secure infrastructure, CSC retains responsibility
for: configuration of customer-controllable settings (IAM,
encryption keys, network ACLs, audit log routing);
authentication of CSC users; classification + handling of
data placed in cloud; CSC-side incident detection (CSP
controls infrastructure; CSC controls workload). CSP-CSC
shared-responsibility matrix per service.

PIMS scope — Privacy Information Management System extends
ISMS to cover Personally Identifiable Information (PII)
processing. Scope must explicitly include PII processing
operations + identify role(s) (controller / processor / both).
Annex A (controllers) + Annex B (processors) provide controls
mapping to ISO/IEC 27002 with privacy-specific guidance.

PII controller controls — 31 controls organised across legal
basis (A.7.2), purpose (A.7.2.2), consent (A.7.2.3-4),
records of PII processing (A.7.2.8), DPIA (A.7.2.5), contract
with PII processor (A.7.2.6), joint controller (A.7.2.7),
subject rights (A.7.3), privacy by design + default (A.7.4),
sharing/transfer (A.7.5). Maps closely to GDPR controller
obligations + CCPA business obligations.

PII processor controls — 18 controls organised across
customer-agreement (B.8.2.1), customer obligations (B.8.2.2),
records of processor PII processing (B.8.2.6), sub-processors
(B.8.5.6-7), PII return + erasure (B.8.4.3). Maps closely to
GDPR Article 28 processor obligations + CCPA §1798.140
service-provider classification.

Certification — PIMS certification is an EXTENSION to ISO/IEC
27001 certification, NOT a standalone. Organisation must
hold valid 27001 cert before pursuing 27701. Combined audit
typical; ISMS scope expanded to include PII processing as
PIMS scope.

Mapping to GDPR + ISO/IEC 29100 — Annex D provides GDPR
Article-by-Article mapping to 27701 clauses + Annex A/B
controls. Annex E maps to ISO/IEC 29100 privacy framework.
Useful for adopters demonstrating GDPR compliance via 27701
certification + for adopters bridging GDPR + CCPA + other
privacy regimes through a single ISMS+PIMS.

Understanding the needs + expectations of interested parties —
determine relevant interested parties (regulators, neighboring
communities, customers, suppliers, workers, NGOs), their relevant
needs + expectations, and which of those become compliance
obligations.

Environmental policy — top management establishes + maintains
a policy appropriate to the purpose + context including the
nature + scale + environmental impacts of activities, products,
services. Includes commitments to protection of the environment
(incl. prevention of pollution + other commitments e.g.,
sustainable resource use, climate change mitigation +
adaptation, biodiversity), fulfillment of compliance
obligations, continual improvement of EMS to enhance
environmental performance.

Environmental aspects — identify aspects of activities, products,
services that can be controlled or influenced; determine
associated environmental impacts considering a lifecycle
perspective. Determine significant environmental aspects
using established criteria. Maintain documented information
of aspects + impacts + criteria + SEAs.

Compliance obligations — determine + have access to the
compliance obligations related to environmental aspects;
determine how these apply to the organization; take obligations
into account when establishing + implementing + maintaining +
continually improving the EMS.

Planning action — plan to take actions to address significant
environmental aspects + compliance obligations + risks +
opportunities identified per §6.1.1, and to evaluate the
effectiveness of these actions. Integration into EMS
processes per §6.1.1.

Environmental objectives + planning to achieve them — establish
at relevant functions + levels, consistent with environmental
policy, considering SEAs + compliance obligations + risks +
opportunities. Measurable, monitored, communicated, updated.

Communication — internal + external communications relevant to
the EMS including: what, when, with whom, how. External
communication of significant environmental information as
established by compliance obligations + the communication
process. Responsiveness to relevant communications received.

Operational planning + control — establish + implement +
control + maintain processes needed to meet EMS requirements
+ implement actions identified in §6.1 + §6.2. Includes
operational criteria for SEAs, control of planned changes,
review of unintended changes + mitigation of adverse effects,
control / influence of outsourced processes, lifecycle
perspective in design + procurement.

Emergency preparedness + response — establish + implement +
maintain processes needed to prepare for + respond to potential
emergency situations identified in §6.1.1. Periodic test of
planned response actions where practicable. Periodic review +
revision based on test results + actual occurrences.

Evaluation of compliance — establish + implement + maintain
processes needed to evaluate fulfillment of compliance
obligations. Determine frequency, evaluate compliance + take
action if needed, maintain knowledge + understanding of
compliance status. Documented information retained as
evidence of evaluation results.

Nonconformity + corrective action — react to nonconformity
including taking action to control + correct it + deal with
consequences (including mitigating adverse environmental
impacts); evaluate need for action to eliminate causes;
implement; review effectiveness; make changes to EMS if
necessary.

Understanding the needs + expectations of workers + other
interested parties — determine + monitor interested parties
(workers, contractors, suppliers, customers, visitors,
regulators, communities, families of workers), their relevant
needs + expectations, which become compliance obligations.

OH&S policy — top management establishes + implements +
maintains a policy that includes commitment to: provide safe
+ healthy working conditions for prevention of work-related
injury + ill-health, appropriate to purpose + size + context
and the specific nature of OH&S risks + opportunities;
provide framework for setting OH&S objectives; fulfil legal
+ other requirements; eliminate hazards + reduce OH&S risks;
continual improvement of OHSMS; consultation + participation
of workers + their representatives.

Consultation + participation of workers — establish + implement
+ maintain processes for consultation + participation of
non-managerial workers (and their representatives where they
exist) in development + planning + implementation + performance
evaluation + actions for improvement of the OHSMS. Provide
mechanisms + time + training + resources; remove + minimize
barriers; specific topics requiring consultation OR
participation are listed in §5.4 a) and b).

Hazard identification + assessment of risks + opportunities —
establish + implement + maintain a hazard identification process
ongoing + proactive. Consider routine + non-routine activities,
workplace, work organization, factors affecting workers
(incl. psychosocial), past relevant incidents, emergency
situations. Assess OH&S risks + identify other risks to the
OHSMS. Identify OH&S opportunities + other opportunities.

Determination of legal + other requirements — determine + have
access to up-to-date legal + other requirements applicable to
hazards + OH&S risks + OHSMS; determine how these requirements
apply + need to be communicated; take into account when
establishing + implementing + maintaining + improving OHSMS.

Planning action — plan to take actions to address risks +
opportunities, address legal + other requirements, prepare
for + respond to emergency situations. Integrate into OHSMS
processes + other business processes. Evaluate effectiveness.

Awareness — workers shall be made aware of the OH&S policy +
objectives, their contribution to OHSMS effectiveness,
implications + consequences of not conforming to OHSMS
requirements, incidents + outcomes of investigations
relevant to them, hazards + OH&S risks + actions
determined relevant to them, ability to remove themselves
from work situations they consider to present an imminent
+ serious danger to their life or health, and arrangements
for protecting them from undue consequences for doing so.

Eliminating hazards + reducing OH&S risks — establish +
implement + maintain a process(es) for the elimination of
hazards + reduction of OH&S risks using the hierarchy of
controls: eliminate the hazard; substitute with less
hazardous processes / operations / materials / equipment;
use engineering controls + reorganization of work;
administrative controls including training; PPE. PPE is
the last resort.

Management of change — establish process(es) for implementation
+ control of planned temporary + permanent changes that
affect OH&S performance (new / modified products / services /
processes; workplace / surroundings / work organization /
working conditions; equipment; workforce; legal + other
requirements; knowledge / information about hazards + OH&S
risks; technology development). Review consequences of
unintended changes + mitigate adverse effects.

Procurement — establish process(es) to control procurement of
products + services so they conform to OHSMS. Includes
coordinating procurement processes with contractors to identify
hazards + assess + control OH&S risks arising from contractors'
activities + operations that impact organization OR workers OR
other interested parties.

Emergency preparedness + response — establish + implement +
maintain process(es) needed to prepare for + respond to
potential emergency situations identified in §6.1.2.1.
Planned response, training, communication of relevant
information to workers + interested parties, periodic testing
+ revision, evaluation + revision after testing + occurrence.

Incident + nonconformity + corrective action — react in a
timely manner to incidents + nonconformities including
controlling + correcting them, dealing with consequences;
evaluate (with participation of workers + involvement of
other relevant interested parties) the need for corrective
action to eliminate root cause(s); review existing
OH&S risk assessments + other risks; determine + implement
action needed including corrective; review effectiveness;
make changes to OHSMS if necessary.

Defect Information Report (DIR) — manufacturer determining
that a safety-related defect or noncompliance with an FMVSS
exists in its products shall furnish notification to NHTSA
within 5 working days. Report content per §573.6(c) includes
manufacturer + product identification, defect/noncompliance
description, hazard assessment, vehicle/equipment population
identification + numbers, remedy program, schedule, owner-
notification plan.

Owner Notification — manufacturer shall send notification by
first-class mail to each owner (per §577.6) within 60 days
of submitting the 573 report (per §577.7). Letter content
per §577.5 includes 10 mandatory elements (manufacturer +
product identification, defect/noncompliance description,
risk to motor vehicle safety, warning against continued use,
remedy description + time for availability, no-charge
remedy statement, instructions + NHTSA complaint procedure,
campaign number). Second notification per §577.8 if remedy
completion < 70% at 6 months. Reimbursement per §577.9 for
pre-notification remedy charges.

TREAD Act Early Warning Reporting — automotive manufacturers
above thresholds (passenger cars > 5,000 units; multipurpose
passenger vehicles + trucks > 25,000 units; etc.) submit
quarterly EWR reports per §579.21 covering: production data;
death + injury + property damage claims; field reports;
consumer complaints; warranty claims; foreign defect
notifications + recalls. Pattern in EWR data may trigger
573 defect determination — the two frameworks are linked.

FDA recall classification — Class I (reasonable probability
that use will cause serious adverse health consequences or
death); Class II (use may cause temporary or medically
reversible adverse health consequences or remote serious
consequences); Class III (use is not likely to cause adverse
health consequences). Voluntary recalls initiated by firm;
FDA classifies after firm submission. Effectiveness checks
per §7.42(b)(4) at three levels (A = 100% / B = sample /
C = ~10%) per Class.

Medical-device Reports of Corrections and Removals —
manufacturers report corrections (e.g., field-software patch)
and removals (e.g., device retrieval) initiated to reduce
risk to health or remedy violation. Within 10 working days
of initiating the action. Report content per §806.10(c)
includes date + description + reason + product identification
+ quantity + consignee identification + risk + copies of
communications. Distinct from MDR adverse-event reports per
21 CFR Part 803.

Substantial Product Hazard reporting — every manufacturer +
importer + distributor + retailer who obtains information
which reasonably supports the conclusion that a product they
market presents a substantial product hazard shall report to
CPSC within 24 hours per §15(b). Substantial product hazard
defined per §15(a) as: (1) failure to comply with a CPSC
rule + the failure creates substantial risk of injury, OR
(2) defect which creates substantial risk of injury. CPSC
reviews + may negotiate corrective action plan + publish
recall notice. 16 CFR Part 1115 provides further detail.

Recall decision flow — single Recall Coordinator decision-
maker convenes multi-functional Recall Team within 4 hours
(1 hour for known Class I / serious-risk / known substantial
product hazard). Team reviews evidence + applies framework-
specific classification + decision documented with rationale
+ time-stamped.

Distribution-list extraction + product traceability —
framework-specific traceability granularity (NHTSA: per-VIN;
FDA medical: per-UDI + per-lot/serial; FDA food: per-lot
+ 1-up-1-down; CPSIA consumer products: per-batch +
per-distributor). Target extraction time ≤ 4 hours after
recall decision.

Effectiveness checks verifying that recall notifications
reached consignees + consignees acted on them. Three FDA
levels per Class (A / B / C); NHTSA quarterly status
reporting per §573.7 with completion rates; CPSC quarterly
progress reports per agreed schedule.

Recovery + disposition — destroyed (with witness verification
+ Certificate of Destruction) OR reworked / reconditioned
(only with regulator agreement) OR returned-to-customer
after retrofit. Tracking units recovered vs. units shipped
with ongoing recovery rate.

Mock recall exercise minimum annually — tests distribution-
list extraction speed + accuracy, lot/VIN/UDI traceability,
team activation + communication, documentation completeness.
Acceptance target ≤ 4 hours for distribution-list completion
(FDA food guidance; NHTSA expects manufacturer-defined
target; medical-device UDI traceability expected near-
immediate).

Integrated framework with 19 domains + 50 control objectives
+ 156 controls (v11.x). Controls are organized into
implementation levels (Level 1-3+) based on organizational
risk factors + regulatory factors (HIPAA + HITECH + state
breach laws + sector-specific regs). HITRUST authoritative
sources cover 40+ frameworks including HIPAA, ISO 27001, NIST
SP 800-53, PCI DSS, GDPR.

MyCSF assessment scoping — organization-specific risk +
regulatory factors drive which controls + implementation
levels apply. Scope determines whether r2 (Risk-based
2-year), e1 (Essentials 1-year), or i1 (Implemented 1-year)
assessment is appropriate.

External assessor — for HITRUST certification (vs. self-
assessment), an authorized External Assessor Firm performs
validated assessment. QA review by HITRUST before
certification issued. Re-assessment cadence per assessment
type.

Multi-framework mapping — HITRUST controls cross-reference
to authoritative sources (HIPAA Security Rule + HITECH +
ISO 27001 Annex A + NIST SP 800-53 + PCI DSS + state privacy
laws + sector regs). One assessment can satisfy multiple
framework requirements through cross-reference reporting.

i1 Intermediate scope — 182 controls representing leading
cybersecurity practices. Static control set (not tailored by
organisation factors as r2 is). 1-year assessment cadence.
Significantly more rigorous than e1 (44 controls) but lower
cost + time than r2 (200-2000+ controls based on factors).

Leading-practices alignment — i1 controls map to NIST
Cybersecurity Framework Implementation Tier 3 + NIST SP
800-171 + ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A baseline + HIPAA Security
Rule comprehensive. Designed as mid-tier assurance for
vendors whose risk profile exceeds e1 but does not warrant
r2 depth + cost.

Validated Assessment Report (VAR) — External Assessor
Organisation conducts assessment per HITRUST MyCSF; HITRUST
validates + issues VAR + certificate. Customer can review VAR
via HITRUST Assessment Exchange (replacing manual VAR
requests). 1-year validity.

Typical i1 adopters — mid-market healthcare-tech with growing
PHI footprint; SaaS providers serving healthcare payers +
providers where annual VAR refresh acceptable; vendors needing
stronger-than-e1 assurance + lower-than-r2 commitment.

Govern (new in v2.0) — organizational context + risk management
strategy + roles/responsibilities + policies + cybersecurity
supply-chain risk management (C-SCRM) + oversight. Establishes
+ monitors + improves the org's cybersecurity risk management
strategy + expectations + policy.

Identify — asset management + business environment + risk
assessment + improvement. Understand cybersecurity risks
to systems + people + assets + data + capabilities.

Protect — identity management + authentication + access
control + awareness + training + data security + platform
security + technology infrastructure resilience. Safeguards
to ensure delivery of critical services.

Detect — continuous monitoring + adverse event analysis.
Discover + analyze cybersecurity events to find anomalies +
indicators of compromise + adverse events that may
compromise systems.

Respond — incident management + analysis + response
reporting + communication + mitigation. Take action regarding
a detected cybersecurity incident.

Recover — incident recovery plan execution + communication.
Restore assets + operations affected by a cybersecurity
incident; lessons learned.

Profiles + Tiers — Organizational Profile describes current
+ target cybersecurity posture; gap analysis between Current
Profile + Target Profile drives improvement priorities.
Tiers (Partial / Risk Informed / Repeatable / Adaptive)
describe the degree to which cybersecurity risk management
practices exhibit characteristics defined in the Framework.

Risk management practices are formally approved + expressed as
organisation-wide policy. Cybersecurity practices are regularly
updated based on application of risk management processes to
changes in business/mission requirements, threats, and
technology landscape.

Organisation-wide approach to manage cybersecurity risk.
Risk-informed policies, processes, procedures defined,
implemented as intended, and reviewed. Consistent methods to
respond effectively to changes in risk. Personnel possess
knowledge + skills to perform their roles.

Organisation understands its role + dependencies + dependents
in larger ecosystem. May contribute to community's broader
understanding of risks. Collaborates with + receives information
regularly from external parties (peers, ISACs, regulators,
supply chain partners); acts on information consistently.

Typical Tier 3 adopters: established mid-market + enterprise
organisations with mature cybersecurity programs; regulated
industries (financial services, healthcare, defense) where
Tier 3 is often a baseline regulatory expectation.
Tier 3 is the most-common TARGET state for
well-resourced cybersecurity programs.

Compliance policy — top management establishes a documented
compliance policy that includes commitment to comply with
applicable obligations + continual improvement of CMS +
protection of whistleblowers from reprisal + sanctions for
non-compliance.

Compliance function — established with independence + authority
+ competence + resources + direct reporting to governing body.
Distinguishable from ISO 37001 anti-bribery compliance function
(which is anti-bribery-specific); ISO 37301 compliance function
is BROADER.

Identification of compliance obligations + risk assessment —
determine + access + maintain + integrate compliance
obligations (laws + regulations + contracts + voluntary
commitments + standards + organizational policies). Compliance
risk assessment per ISO 31000 framework.

Operational planning + control + establishment of controls —
financial + non-financial controls; procurement + contracting
controls; outsourcing arrangements; controls on training +
awareness + communication.

Annex SL baseline — general-business profile leverages
ISO 37301's Annex SL structure for clean integration with
other Annex SL standards (ISO 9001 quality + ISO 14001
environmental + ISO 45001 OH&S + ISO 50001 energy + ISO
27001 information security + ISO 22301 BC + ISO 37001
anti-bribery + ISO 31000 risk meta-framework). Common
integration mode: combined IMS audit with shared management
review.

Product safety + consumer law — general-business compliance
programmes integrate product-safety + consumer-law obligations
(EU GPSR for consumer products; CPSC for US consumer products;
FTC Act §5 deceptive practices; EU UCPD unfair commercial
practices; state consumer-protection acts). Often composes
eu-gpsr + recall-workflow + privacy overlays.

Tax + trade compliance — corporate tax + VAT/GST/sales-tax +
transfer pricing (OECD BEPS Pillar 1+2) + country-by-country
reporting; export controls (US EAR + ITAR; EU Dual-Use
Regulation 2021/821); sanctions (OFAC + EU + UN);
anti-boycott (US EAR Part 760); customs + trade-agreement
origin determination.

Competition + antitrust — Sherman Act + Clayton Act + FTC
Act §5 (US); TFEU Articles 101-102 + Block Exemption
Regulations (EU); national competition acts; merger control
(HSR Act US + EU Merger Regulation + national merger control);
cartel-prevention compliance programmes; pricing + supply +
distribution restrictions.

Energy policy — top management establishes + implements +
maintains an energy policy that is appropriate to the
organization's purpose, provides framework for setting +
reviewing energy objectives + targets, includes commitment
to ensure information + necessary resources for achieving
the objectives + targets, commitment to satisfy applicable
legal + other requirements related to energy efficiency +
use + consumption, commitment to continual improvement of
energy performance + the EnMS, supports procurement of
energy-efficient products + services + design activities
to improve energy performance.

Energy objectives + planning to achieve them — establish energy
objectives at relevant functions + levels + processes +
facilities. Consistent with energy policy + measurable + take
into account applicable legal + other requirements + consider
SEUs + consider opportunities to improve energy performance.
Monitored + communicated + updated as appropriate.

Energy review — develop + record + maintain an energy review
based on measurement + other data: analyze energy use +
consumption based on measurement + other data, identify
Significant Energy Uses (SEUs) based on energy use +
consumption + criteria, determine current energy performance
of facilities + equipment + systems + processes + personnel
affecting SEUs, identify + prioritize + record opportunities
for improving energy performance + for changing in the future
energy use + consumption.

Energy performance indicators (EnPIs) — determine EnPIs
appropriate for measuring + monitoring energy performance,
including methodology for determining + updating EnPIs.
EnPI values shall be reviewed + compared to corresponding
energy baselines. Documented information of EnPI methodology
+ values + measures + their changes.

Energy baseline (EnB) — establish EnB(s) using information
from energy review considering a suitable period of data.
Changes to EnPIs shall be measured against the corresponding
EnB. EnB(s) shall be revised in the case of: EnPI(s) no
longer reflecting organizational energy performance;
major changes to static factors; significant changes to
operations + processes + energy systems. Maintained as
documented information.

Planning for collection of energy data — ensure that the key
characteristics of operations affecting energy performance
are identified + measured + monitored + analyzed at planned
intervals. Energy data collection plan addresses: relevant
variables related to SEUs, energy consumption related to
SEUs + the organization, operational criteria related to
SEUs, static factors (if applicable), data specified in
action plans. Data + methods recorded + reviewed + updated.

Operational planning + control — plan + implement + control
processes related to SEUs by establishing criteria for
effective operation + maintenance of SEUs (the absence of
such criteria could lead to a significant deviation from
effective energy performance), operating + maintaining
facilities + equipment + systems + processes in accordance
with operational criteria, communicating operational
controls to relevant persons. Control of planned changes.
Review of consequences of unintended changes + mitigation
of adverse effects.

Design — consider energy performance improvement opportunities
+ operational control in design of new, modified, and
renovated facilities + equipment + systems + processes that
can have significant impact on energy performance over the
planned or expected operating lifetime. Results of energy
performance considerations shall be incorporated into
specification + design + procurement activities.

Procurement — establish + implement criteria for assessing
energy performance over the planned or expected operating
lifetime when procuring energy-using products + equipment +
services that are expected to have significant impact on
organization's energy performance. Inform suppliers that
procurement is partly evaluated on basis of energy
performance. For procurement of energy: define + document
specifications, as applicable, for purchased energy.

Monitoring + measurement + analysis + evaluation of energy
performance + the EnMS — key characteristics determined +
monitored at planned intervals, including effectiveness
of action plans in achieving objectives + targets, EnPIs,
operation of SEUs, actual vs. expected energy consumption.
EnPI values investigated + responded to where significant
deviations occur. Documented information retained.

Nonconformity + corrective action — react to nonconformity
(incl. taking action to control + correct it, dealing with
consequences); evaluate need for action to eliminate root
cause(s); implement; review effectiveness; make changes to
EnMS if necessary. Documented information retained as
evidence of NC + actions + results.
